title: Travelers Value Sustainability — But Only If It's Cheap
paragraphs: Sustainability is becoming an important part of people's travel choices. And that doesn't just mean avoiding damage to the local environment and historical sites — it also means helping to support local communities and economies in the places they visit.
In fact, 75% of travelers now say sustainability is important when making travel decisions.
That's according to a survey of almost 8,800 people around the world by online travel agency Trip.com.

However, while three-quarters of survey participants said sustainability is important, only 57% said they intentionally choose more sustainable options — so there's a gap between what people think and what they do.

Participants said things that keep them from making more sustainable travel choices include higher prices, inconvenience or the need to put in extra effort, as well as the difficulty of finding sustainable options.
And while almost 60% of travelers said they would be OK paying more for sustainable travel, fewer than one in 10 would pay over 10% more.

When asked what drives them to make more sustainable travel choices, the most common answer, given by 53% of participants, was that they feel a sense of "environmental responsibility." Fifty-one percent also named the need to preserve destinations for future generations, while 44% said they want "more authentic travel experiences."

In fact, many people don't just see sustainable travel as a responsibility — they think it can make their travel experience better. Sustainable options that people think could improve their trips include things like exploring nature and outdoor destinations, scenic rail journeys, and visiting less-known destinations with fewer crowds.

However, when asked what matters most when planning a trip, sustainability was still far from the top of the list. Sixty-four percent said price is one of the most important things they think about, while 62% named quality and comfort, and 42% named convenience.
The environmental and social impact of a trip was chosen by just 22%.
